claim: About one third of all newly synthesized proteins pass through the ER.
source: It is estimated that about one third of all newly synthesized proteins pass through the ER, where they fold and assemble into multi-subunit complexes, and where post-translational modifications such as disulfide bridge formation and glycosylation occur (Braakman and Hebert, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Braakman and Hebert, 2013, indicating reliance on published literature.

claim: Three principal transmembrane sensors of the UPR independently monitor folding stress in the ER: IRE1, PERK and ATF6.
source: Three principal transmembrane sensors of the UPR independently monitor folding stress in the ER – IRE1, PERK and ATF6 (Gardner et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gardner et al., 2013.

claim: ATF6 is a membrane-tethered transcription factor activated by regulated trafficking and proteolysis producing ATF6-N.
source: ATF6 is a membrane-tethered transcription factor activated by regulated trafficking and proteolysis producing ATF6-N, the ATF6 fragment that constitutes the functional transcription factor (Haze et al., 1999; Ye et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haze et al., 1999; Ye et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2002.

claim: IRE1 removes an intron from the mRNA encoding the UPR effector XBP1 allowing translation of XBP1s.
source: In contrast, the highly conserved kinase-endoribonuclease IRE1 removes an intron from the mRNA encoding the UPR effector XBP1 allowing translation of XBP1s ('s' for spliced), the functional transcription factor variant of this protein (Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yoshida et al., 2001.

claim: ATF6 upregulates transcription of chaperones, foldases and lipid synthesis genes.
source: ATF6 upregulates transcription of chaperones, foldases and lipid synthesis genes (Wu et al., 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2007; Adachi et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2007; Adachi et al., 2008.

claim: XBP1 upregulates ER chaperones and the ERAD machinery.
source: while XBP1 upregulates ER chaperones and the ERAD machinery (Lee et al., 2003; Acosta-Alvear et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2003; Acosta-Alvear et al., 2007.

claim: Regulated IRE1-dependent mRNA decay (RIDD) cleaves ER-targeted mRNAs leading to their degradation.
source: Regulated IRE1-dependent mRNA decay (RIDD) cleaves ER-targeted mRNAs leading to their degradation (Hollien et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hollien et al., 2009.

claim: PERK phosphorylates the α-subunit of the initiation factor (eIF2-α) leading to transient inhibition of cap-dependent translation.
source: PERK, a second transmembrane kinase, phosphorylates itself and the α-subunit of the initiation factor (eIF2-α) leading to transient inhibition of cap-dependent translation and an increase in translation of UPR effectors with upstream open reading frames (Harding et al., 1999; Sidrauski et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harding et al., 1999; Sidrauski et al., 2015.

claim: Both IRE1 and ATF6 signaling attenuate after prolonged ER stress.
source: Both IRE1 and ATF6 signaling attenuate after prolonged ER stress, removing most of the cytoprotective functions of the UPR (Lin et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2014; Haze et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2014; Haze et al., 2001.

claim: PERK signaling is maintained after prolonged ER stress and commits the cell to apoptosis through CHOP.
source: PERK signaling is maintained and, through CHOP, commits the cell to apoptosis (Zinszner et al., 1998; Palam et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zinszner et al., 1998; Palam et al., 2011.

claim: Many small molecule inhibitors and activators of the PERK and IRE1 enzymes have been isolated.
source: Many small molecule inhibitors and activators of the PERK and IRE1 enzymes have been isolated (Maly and Papa, 2014; Maurel et al., 2015; Mendez et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maly and Papa, 2014; Maurel et al., 2015; Mendez et al., 2015.

claim: No pharmacological agents promoting the selective modulation of ATF6 have been developed prior to this work.
source: In contrast, no pharmacological agents promoting the selective modulation of ATF6 have been developed, in part due to the fact that, unlike IRE1 and PERK, ATF6 is not an enzyme.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of prior reports in the literature and the reasoning that ATF6 is not an enzyme.

claim: ATF6α and ATF6β act redundantly during development as single knockout mice are viable and fertile while double knockout animals are pre-implantation lethal.
source: ATF6α and ATF6β act redundantly during development as single knockout mice are viable and fertile while double knockout animals are pre-implantation lethal (Yamamoto et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yamamoto et al., 2007.

claim: ATF6α and ATF6β do not appear to act redundantly during ER stress as ATF6α knockout cells or animals die when challenged with ER stressors.
source: Conversely, ATF6α and ATF6β do not appear to act redundantly during ER stress as ATF6α knockout cells or animals die when challenged with ER stressors (Wu et al., 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2007.

claim: Upon ER stress ATF6 moves from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.
source: Regulation of ATF6 signaling is by spatial separation of the substrate, ATF6, in the ER and the proteases, site-1 and site-2 proteases (S1P and S2P, respectively), in the Golgi apparatus: upon ER stress ATF6 moves from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of ATF6 activation.

claim: The transport of ATF6 from the ER to the Golgi requires the COPII coat.
source: The mechanism by which ATF6 trafficking is regulated is poorly understood but the transport requires the COPII coat (Nadanaka et al., 2004; Schindler and Schekman, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nadanaka et al., 2004; Schindler and Schekman, 2009.

claim: Inhibition of ATF6 was achieved by inhibiting the proteases S1P and S2P.
source: Inhibition of ATF6 was achieved by inhibiting the proteases that release it from the membrane – S1P and S2P, respectively (Ye et al., 2000; Okada et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ye et al., 2000; Okada et al., 2003.

claim: S1P and S2P proteases also play essential roles in regulating cholesterol homeostasis via processing of SREBP.
source: These proteases do not uniquely process ATF6 but also play essential roles in regulating cholesterol homeostasis via processing of SREBP (Brown and Goldstein, 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brown and Goldstein, 1997.

claim: S1P and S2P proteases play essential roles in lysosome biogenesis via processing of the α/β-subunit precursor of the N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase complex.
source: and lysosome biogenesis via processing of the α/β-subunit precursor of the N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase complex (Marschner et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marschner et al., 2011.

claim: The pleiotropic engagement of S1P and S2P limits the usefulness of S1P and S2P inhibitors for studies of the UPR.
source: Their pleiotropic engagement limits the usefulness of S1P and S2P inhibitors for studies of the UPR.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the multiple roles of S1P and S2P.

claim: The authors developed cell-based screens to identify a series of pyrazole amides as the first selective inhibitors of the ATF6α branch of the UPR.
source: Here we developed cell-based screens to identify a series of pyrazole amides as the first selective inhibitors of the ATF6α branch of the UPR.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ceapins trap ATF6α in the ER in discrete foci.
source: We show in the accompanying manuscript that these compounds trap ATF6α in the ER in discrete foci, which inspired us to name the compounds 'Ceapins' from the Irish verb 'ceap' meaning 'to trap' (Gallagher and Walter, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to an accompanying manuscript (Gallagher and Walter, 2016).

claim: Ceapins do not inhibit activation of either IRE1 or PERK in response to ER stress.
source: Ceapins do not inhibit activation of either IRE1 or PERK in response to ER stress
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ceapins do not inhibit trafficking and cleavage of SREBP in response to low sterols.
source: nor do they inhibit trafficking and cleavage of SREBP in response to low sterols
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ceapins do not inhibit trafficking and cleavage of ATF6β in response to ER stress.
source: or ATF6β in response to ER stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Through structure-activity studies the authors increased the potency of the Ceapin series ten-fold to an IC50 of 600 nM.
source: Through structure-activity studies we increased the potency of the series ten-fold to an IC50 of 600 nM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Inhibition of ATF6α with Ceapin analogs has no toxicity in unstressed cells.
source: Inhibition of ATF6α with Ceapin analogs has no toxicity in unstressed cells
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Inhibition of ATF6α with Ceapin analogs increases the sensitivity of cells to ER stress inducers.
source: but increases the sensitivity of cells to ER stress inducers, closely mimicking the genetic ablation of ATF6α in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: The authors cloned two copies of the ER stress response element (ERSE) upstream of a minimal promoter driving expression of luciferase into a retroviral vector.
source: To this end, we cloned two copies of the ER stress response element (ERSE) upstream of a minimal promoter driving expression of luciferase (Figure 1A) into a retroviral vector
evidence: The claim is supported by the description in the text and the schematic in Figure 1A.

claim: The authors generated a HEK293T-based ERSE-luciferase reporter stable cell line.
source: which we used to generate a HEK293T-based ERSE-luciferase reporter stable cell line.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the methods used.

claim: Treatment of the reporter cells with thapsigargin causes a 3.8 ± 0.2-fold induction of luciferase activity.
source: ER stress causes a 3.8 ± 0.2-fold induction of luciferase activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ER stress-induced luciferase was not affected by inhibition of IRE1.
source: The ER stress-induced luciferase was not affected by inhibition of IRE1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Patterson et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Patterson et al., 2011.

claim: The ERSE-luciferase cell line reports selectively on the ATF6 branch.
source: indicating that the cell line reported selectively on the ATF6 branch.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that IRE1 inhibition does not affect the reporter.

claim: The authors screened 106,281 compounds at a single concentration for their ability to inhibit Tg-induced luciferase activity in the reporter cells.
source: We screened 106,281 compounds at a single concentration for their ability to inhibit Tg-induced luciferase activity in the reporter cells (Figure 1C, see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for overview of screen workflow).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description in the text and data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: About 1% of the compounds (1142) showed >69% inhibition in the primary screen.
source: About 1% of the compounds (1142) showed >69% inhibition (amounting to three standard deviations from the mean of stressed controls).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data from the primary screen shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When fresh stocks were retested in dose response assays, all 598 remaining compounds showed inhibitory activity with an IC50 < 13.5 μM against Tg-induced luciferase activity in the reporter cells.
source: When fresh stocks were retested in dose response assays, all 598 remaining compounds showed inhibitory activity with an IC50 < 13.5 μM against Tg-induced luciferase activity in the reporter cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the secondary screening results.

claim: Sixty of the 598 compounds isolated in the primary screen inhibited doxycycline-induced MPZ-GFP expression and were removed from further consideration.
source: Sixty of the 598 compounds isolated in the primary screen inhibited doxycycline-induced MPZ-GFP expression and were removed from further consideration
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the counter-screening results.

claim: The authors isolated a collection of 538 compounds that inhibited ER stress-induced ATF6 signaling without inhibiting either transcription or translation or inhibiting signaling through other UPR branches.
source: yielding a collection of 538 compounds that inhibited ER stress-induced ATF6 signaling without inhibiting either transcription or translation or inhibiting signaling through other UPR branches.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the screening and counter-screening results.

claim: In unstressed cells, GFP-ATF6α colocalized with GRP94, indicating its predominant localization in the ER.
source: In unstressed cells, GFP-ATF6α colocalized with GRP94, indicating its predominant localization in the ER (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the image data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Upon ER stress, GFP-ATF6α translocated to the nucleus and colocalized with DNA.
source: Upon ER stress, GFP-ATF6α translocated to the nucleus and colocalized with DNA (Figure 2B, yellow in merged image).
evidence: The claim is supported by the image data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When ATF6 cleavage by S1P was inhibited, GFP-ATF6α no longer translocated to the nucleus but accumulated in perinuclear punctae, corresponding to the Golgi apparatus.
source: As a positive control, when we inhibited ATF6 cleavage by S1P, GFP-ATF6α no longer translocated to the nucleus but accumulated in perinuclear punctae, corresponding to the Golgi apparatus (Figure 2C, see also Figure 3 in Gallagher and Walter (2016)).
evidence: The claim is supported by the image data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to Gallagher and Walter (2016).

claim: Ceapin-A1 shows decreased nuclear GFP signal and perinuclear GFP-ATF6α punctae.
source: Figure 2D shows Ceapin-A1 as an example in this class showing decreased nuclear GFP signal and perinuclear GFP-ATF6α punctae.
evidence: The claim is supported by the image data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Statistical evaluation of unstressed and stressed controls yielded a mean Z' of 0.7 +/- 0.18 for the nuclear translocation assay.
source: Statistical evaluation of unstressed and stressed controls yielded a mean Z' of 0.7 +/- 0.18, which is an exceptionally robust read-out for a cell- and image-based high-throughput assay.
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the assay controls shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Of 598 compounds tested, 85 showed robust inhibition of ER stress-induced nuclear translocation of GFP-ATF6α above three standard deviations from the mean of the negative control.
source: Of 598 compounds tested in this way, 85 showed robust inhibition of ER stress-induced nuclear translocation of GFP- ATF6α above three standard deviations from the mean of the negative (Tg-alone) control.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the nuclear translocation assay results.

claim: After completion of secondary assays, the authors were left with 38 Class 1 and 128 Class 2 inhibitors, of which 29 and 70 were repurchased.
source: After completion of these assays, we were left with 38 Class 1 and 128 Class 2 inhibitors, of which 29 and 70 were repurchased.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the compound triage process.

claim: Of 99 repurchased compounds, 98 showed inhibitory activity with Tg, of which 82 also inhibited tunicamycin induced ERSE-luciferase.
source: Of 99 repurchased compounds, 98 showed inhibitory activity with Tg, of which 82 also inhibited tunicamycin induced ERSE-luciferase.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the tertiary screening results.

claim: Of the Class 1 inhibitors, only Ceapin-A1 consistently blocked ATF6α target gene upregulation.
source: Of the Class 1 inhibitors, only one consistently blocked ATF6α target gene upregulation: Ceapin-A1
evidence: The claim is supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ceapin-A1 inhibited both ERSE-luciferase induction by both Tg and Tm and induction of GRP78 mRNA with an IC50 = 4.7 ± 1.1 μM.
source: Ceapin-A1 inhibited both ERSE-luciferase induction by both Tg (Figure 3A) and Tm (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and induction of GRP78 mRNA (Figure 3B) with an IC50 = 4.7 ± 1.1 μM
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, Figure 3B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ceapin-A1 inhibited ATF6α target gene upregulation to the same extent as the S1P inhibitor.
source: and to the same extent as the S1P inhibitor.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3B.

claim: Inhibition of IRE1 had little effect on ERSE-luciferase induction or GRP78 mRNA induction.
source: Inhibition of IRE1 (Cross et al., 2012) had little effect in the same assays (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3B, and a citation to Cross et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of the integrated stress response (ISR) showed a decrease in ATF6α target gene induction.
source: In contrast, inhibition of the integrated stress response (ISR) (Sidrauski et al., 2013) showed a decrease in ATF6α target gene induction, as previously reported for PERK knockout cells (Wu et al., 2007) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citations to Sidrauski et al., 2013 and Wu et al., 2007.

claim: Addition of Ceapin-A1 to 25 μM had no effect on lipoprotein depletion-mediated SREBP processing.
source: Addition of Ceapin-A1 to 25 μM (> five times its IC50) had no effect on lipoprotein depletion-mediated SREBP processing (Figure 3C, lanes 3–6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ceapin-A1 neither inhibits S1P nor S2P.
source: Therefore, Ceapin-A1 neither inhibits S1P nor S2P
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that Ceapin-A1 does not inhibit SREBP processing.

claim: Ceapin-A1 emerges as the first small molecule inhibitor of ATF6 that does not inhibit SREBP or other pathways known to use S1P and S2P proteases.
source: and emerges as the first small molecule inhibitor of ATF6 that does not inhibit SREBP or other pathways known to use these proteases.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing selectivity of Ceapin-A1.

claim: Induction of ER stress led to cleavage of full-length ATF6α to produce the faster migrating, active transcription factor ATF6α-N.
source: Induction of ER stress led to cleavage of full-length ATF6α to produce the faster migrating, active transcription factor ATF6α-N (Figure 3D, lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the presence of the S1P inhibitor, ER stress-induced cleavage of ATF6α was not blocked.
source: Surprisingly, in the presence of the S1P inhibitor, ER stress-induced cleavage of ATF6α was not blocked (Figure 3D, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The cleavage product produced in the presence of the S1P inhibitor (ATF6α-M) migrated more slowly on SDS polyacrylamide gels than the product ATF6α-N produced by ER stress alone.
source: As a first clue on how to resolve the paradox, we observed that the cleavage product, henceforth referred to as ATF6α-M, produced in the presence of the S1P inhibitor migrated more slowly on SDS polyacrylamide gels than the product ATF6α-N produced by ER stress alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In cells treated with ER stress inducer and the S1P inhibitor, both ATF6α and ATF6α-M were recovered in the membrane fraction.
source: In contrast to ER stressed cells, where ATF6α was recovered in the membrane fraction (Figure 3D, lane 12) and ATF6α-N is in the nuclear fraction (Figure 3D, lane 7), both ATF6α and ATF6α-M were recovered in in the membrane fraction in cells treated with ER stress inducer and the S1P inhibitor (Figure 3D, lane 14).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ATF6α-M remains membrane-bound and as such is incapable of entering the nucleus and activating ATF6α target genes.
source: We therefore denoted this fragment as ATF6α-M, since it remains membrane-bound and as such is incapable of entering the nucleus and activating ATF6α target genes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the subcellular localization data.

claim: An alternate protease generated ATF6α-M and ATF6α-M was not a substrate for subsequent membrane-release by S2P cleavage.
source: We observed the same fragment in cells expressing a variant of ATF6α, in which the S1P cleavage site was mutated (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), indicating that an alternate protease generated ATF6α-M and that ATF6α-M was not a substrate for subsequent membrane-release by S2P cleavage.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cells treated with both ER stress inducer and Ceapin-A1 did not show any ATF6α cleavage product.
source: Importantly, cells treated with both ER stress inducer and Ceapin-A1 did not show any ATF6α cleavage product (Figure 3D, lanes 5, 10, 15).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The mechanism of inhibition of ATF6α processing by Ceapin-A1 is not via protease inhibition, but that ATF6α is trapped in a place or state where it cannot be cleaved.
source: This difference strongly suggested that the mechanism of inhibition of ATF6α processing by Ceapin-A1 is not via protease inhibition, but that ATF6α is trapped in a place or state where it cannot be cleaved.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: All four rings present in Ceapin-A1 are necessary for activity.
source: We found that all four rings present in Ceapin-A1 are necessary for activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Deletion of the furan ring (as in Ceapin-A2) led to a loss of detectable activity in the ERSE-luciferase assay.
source: Thus, deletion of the furan ring (as in Ceapin-A2) led to a loss of detectable activity in the ERSE-luciferase assay.
evidence: The claim is supported by structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Among several aryl and heteroaryl rings examined in place of the furan, only a simple phenyl ring as in Ceapin-A3 (IC50 6.9 ± 0.7) afforded activity comparable to Ceapin-A1 (IC50 = 4.9 ± 1.2 μM).
source: Among several aryl and heteroaryl rings examined in place of the furan, only a simple phenyl ring as in Ceapin-A3 (IC50 6.9 ± 0.7) afforded activity comparable to Ceapin-A1 (IC50 = 4.9 ± 1.2 μM).
evidence: The claim is supported by structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Analogs lacking the ortho and para chloro substituents (Ceapin-A4) or bearing methyl in place of the benzyl group (Ceapin-A5) were inactive.
source: Thus, analogs lacking the ortho and para chloro substituents (Ceapin-A4) or bearing methyl in place of the benzyl group (Ceapin-A5) were inactive (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4D.

claim: Substitution at both the ortho and para position with spheroid hydrophobes was optimal for activity.
source: Further SAR of ring substitution in the benzyl side chain revealed that substitution at both the ortho and para position with spheroid hydrophobes was optimal for activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The 2,4-dibromobenzyl analog Ceapin-A6 was about two-fold more potent than Ceapin-A1.
source: Thus, the 2,4-dibromobenzyl analog Ceapin-A6 was about two-fold more potent than Ceapin-A1
evidence: The claim is supported by structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The bis-trifluoromethyl congener Ceapin-A7 (IC50 = 0.59 ± 0.17 μM) was approximately ten-fold more potent than Ceapin-A1.
source: while the corresponding bis-trifluoromethyl congener Ceapin-A7 (IC50 = 0.59 ± 0.17 μM) was approximately ten-fold more potent than Ceapin-A1 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4D.

claim: Analogs bearing a single trifluoromethyl group at either the para (Ceapin-A8) or ortho position (Ceapin-A9) were notably less potent than Ceapin-A7.
source: In contrast, analogs bearing a single trifluoromethyl group at either the para (Ceapin-A8) or ortho position (Ceapin-A9) were notably less potent than Ceapin-A7.
evidence: The claim is supported by structure-activity relationship data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The mean IC50 values for the S1P inhibitor, Ceapin-A1 and Ceapin-A7 calculated from dose-response qPCR assays correlated well with the values obtained using the ERSE-luciferase reporter.
source: The mean IC50 values for the S1P inhibitor, Ceapin-A1 and Ceapin-A7 calculated from dose-response qPCR assays correlated well with the values obtained using the ERSE-luciferase reporter (Figure 4F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4F.

claim: The inactive Ceapin analog A5 does not inhibit induction of ATF6α target genes.
source: As expected, the inactive Ceapin analog A5 does not inhibit induction of these targets (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The increased IC50 values for HERPUD1 reflect the contribution from the IRE1/XBP1 and PERK/ATF4 branches to transcriptional upregulation of this target.
source: The increased IC50 values for HERPUD1 reflect the contribution from the IRE1/XBP1 and PERK/ATF4 branches to transcriptional upregulation of this target (Lee et al., 2003; Ma and Hendershot, 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2003; Ma and Hendershot, 2004 and the experimental data.

claim: Treatment of cells with Tm produced both a faster migrating unglycosylated form of ATF6α (ATF6α*) and cleaved ATF6α-N.
source: As expected, treatment of cells with Tm produced both a faster migrating unglycosylated form of ATF6α (ATF6α*) and cleaved ATF6α-N (Figure 5A, compare lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cells treated with both Tm and Ceapin-A7 contained the unglycosylated form of ATF6α but not ATF6α-N.
source: Cells treated with both Tm and Ceapin-A7 contained the unglycosylated form of ATF6α but not ATF6α-N (Figure 5A, lane 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ceapin-A7 but not the inactive Ceapin analog A5 inhibited ER stress-induced upregulation of BiP.
source: Consistent with our qPCR analysis of its mRNA levels (GRP78 mRNA), Ceapin-A7 but not the inactive Ceapin analog A5 inhibited ER stress-induced upregulation of BiP (Figure 5B, compare lanes 3 and 7 to lanes 4 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ceapin-A7 did not inhibit activation of either the PERK or the IRE1 branches of the UPR.
source: Ceapin-A7 did not inhibit activation of either the PERK (shown by a slower migrating band representing the phosphorylated form of PERK [Harding et al., 1999]) or the IRE1 (shown by production of XBP1s protein) branches of the UPR.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Harding et al., 1999.

claim: Ceapin-A1 inhibited cleavage of FLAG-ATF6α without inhibiting induction of ATF4 or autophosphorylation of PERK.
source: Ceapin-A1 inhibited cleavage of FLAG-ATF6α without inhibiting induction of ATF4 (Figure 3D, compare lanes 6, 7 and 10) or autophosphorylation of PERK (indicated by the shift in mobility; Figure 3D, compare lanes 11, 12 and 15).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Co-incubation of cells with ER stressor and either S1P inhibitor or Ceapin-A1 showed only a partial decrease in upregulation of XBP1s and DDIT3 mRNA.
source: Consistent with Ceapin inhibiting the ATF6-branch selectively, co-incubation of cells with ER stressor and either S1P inhibitor or Ceapin-A1 showed only a partial decrease in upregulation of XBP1s and DDIT3 mRNA (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The partial decrease in upregulation of XBP1s and DDIT3 mRNA by Ceapin is in agreement with data from ATF6α knockout mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF).
source: in agreement with data from ATF6α knockout mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) (Wu et al., 2007; Adachi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2007; Adachi et al., 2008.

claim: Ceapins are selective inhibitors of the ATF6 branch of the UPR and do not inhibit either IRE1 or PERK signaling.
source: Taken together, these data show that Ceapins are selective inhibitors of the ATF6 branch of the UPR and do not inhibit either IRE1 or PERK signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on the cumulative experimental data presented.

claim: ATF6β is activated with similar kinetics and in response to the same stressors as ATF6α.
source: ATF6β is activated with similar kinetics and in response to the same stressors as ATF6α
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of ATF6β.

claim: ATF6β moves from the ER to the Golgi apparatus where it is processed by S1P and S2P to release ATF6β-N from the membrane allowing its nuclear translocation.
source: and, as ATF6α, moves from the ER to the Golgi apparatus where it is processed by S1P and S2P to release ATF6β-N from the membrane allowing its nuclear translocation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of ATF6β activation.

claim: Ceapin-A7 had no effect on the production of ATF6β-N, even at the highest concentration (18.9 μM; corresponding to 33x its IC50 for ATF6α).
source: In contrast, Ceapin-A7 had no effect on the production of ATF6β-N, even at the highest concentration (18.9 μM; corresponding to 33x its IC50 for ATF6α) (Figure 5D, lanes 17–20 and 24–27).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: While ATF6β-N is not present in nuclear extracts of ER stressed cells treated with S1P inhibitor, cells subjected to ER stress in the absence or presence of Ceapin-A7 both have nuclear localized ATF6β-N.
source: We further confirmed that while ATF6β-N is not present in nuclear extracts of ER stressed cells treated with S1P inhibitor, cells subjected to ER stress in the absence or presence of Ceapin-A7 both have nuclear localized ATF6β-N (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: ATF6α knockout mice and MEF cells show impaired survival in the face of acute or chronic ER stress.
source: ATF6α knockout mice and MEF cells show impaired survival in the face of acute (Yamamoto et al., 2007) or chronic (Wu et al., 2007) ER stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yamamoto et al., 2007 and Wu et al., 2007.

claim: Cells co-incubated with both Tg and Ceapin-A7 showed an almost two-fold increase in sensitivity to ER stress (IC50 = 4.5 nM).
source: Cells co-incubated with both Tg and Ceapin-A7 showed an almost two-fold increase in sensitivity to ER stress (IC50 = 4.5 nM)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6B.

claim: The inactive Ceapin analog A5 showed no difference in cell viability compared to Tg alone.
source: whereas the inactive Ceapin analog A5 showed no difference (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The two-fold difference in sensitivity to ER stress with Ceapin-A7 is consistent with the data from genetic ablation of ATF6α in mice.
source: This two-fold difference is consistent with the data from genetic ablation of ATF6α in mice (Yamamoto et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yamamoto et al., 2007.

claim: Cells treated with Ceapin-A7 alone showed no difference in cell death compared to vehicle alone.
source: Cells treated with Ceapin-A7 alone showed no difference in cell death compared to vehicle alone, consistent with previous work demonstrating that homozygous ATF6α knockout mice are viable and fertile (Wu et al., 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and citations to Wu et al., 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2007.

claim: At low concentrations of ER stress (10 nM Tg), inhibition of ATF6α did not enhance cytotoxicity.
source: At low concentrations of ER stress (10 nM Tg), inhibition of ATF6α did not enhance cytotoxicity
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: As the concentration of ER stressor was increased (30 nM and 90 nM), ATF6α inhibition resulted in a two-fold increase in apoptotic cells compared to cells treated with ER stressor alone.
source: however as the concentration of ER stressor was increased (30 nM and 90 nM), ATF6α inhibition resulted in a two-fold increase in apoptotic cells compared to cells treated with ER stressor alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Human cells treated with ER stress and Ceapin-A7 phenocopy the results obtained using genetic ablation of ATF6α in mouse models.
source: Thus human cells treated with ER stress and Ceapin-A7 phenocopy the results obtained using genetic ablation of ATF6α in mouse models.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparison of experimental data with published results from genetic studies.

claim: Ceapins define a first-in-class series of ATF6α inhibitors that selectively blocks ATF6α and not ATF6β, SREBP or other UPR branches without relying on inhibition of the proteases.
source: Ceapins therefore define a first-in-class series of ATF6α inhibitors that selectively blocks ATF6α and not ATF6β, SREBP or other UPR branches without relying on inhibition of the proteases that are also used by other critical signaling pathways.
evidence: The claim is based on the cumulative experimental data presented.

claim: ATF6 was considered 'undruggable' prior to this work.
source: Indeed, ATF6 was considered 'undruggable' (Maly and Papa, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maly and Papa, 2014.

claim: Ceapins induce rapid, reversible clustering of ATF6α, preventing exit of ATF6α from the ER.
source: As we detail in the accompanying manuscript, Ceapins induce rapid, reversible clustering of ATF6α, preventing exit of ATF6α from the ER (Gallagher and Walter, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to an accompanying manuscript (Gallagher and Walter, 2016).

claim: ATF6α was shown to be required for the survival of dormant tumor cells.
source: ATF6α was shown to be required for the survival of dormant tumor cells (Schewe and Aguirre-Ghiso, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schewe and Aguirre-Ghiso, 2008.

claim: In a cystic fibrosis model, knockdown of ATF6α was shown to increase delivery of the poorly folded △F508 variant of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator to the plasma membrane where it could function.
source: In a cystic fibrosis model, knockdown of ATF6α was shown to increase delivery of the poorly folded △F508 variant of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator to the plasma membrane where it could function (Kerbiriou et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kerbiriou et al., 2007.

claim: Enhancing ATF6α activity using inducible activation of ATF6α-N increased quality control of protein folding in the ER and decreased secretion and extracellular aggregation of amyloidogenic proteins involved in light chain amyloidosis.
source: In contrast, enhancing ATF6α activity using inducible activation of ATF6α-N increased quality control of protein folding in the ER and decreased secretion and extracellular aggregation of amyloidogenic proteins involved in light chain amyloidosis (Cooley et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cooley et al., 2014.

claim: Both PERK and ATF6 act downstream of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) mediated cell survival and angiogenesis.
source: For example, both PERK and ATF6 act downstream of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) mediated cell survival and angiogenesis (Karali et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Karali et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibition of IRE1 alone in models of diabetes led to hyper-activation of ATF6 that led to severe nephropathy.
source: Additionally, inhibition of IRE1 alone in models of diabetes led to hyper-activation of ATF6 that led to severe nephropathy (Madhusudhan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Madhusudhan et al., 2015.

claim: With the identification of Ceapins, we finally have tools to modulate all three branches of the UPR.
source: With the identification of Ceapins, we finally have tools to modulate all three branches and to unleash the full potential of UPR modulation that has remained theoretical up to this point.
evidence: The claim is based on the development of Ceapins as described in the manuscript.
